definitions.definition: A difference between two things that are otherwise the same, like a mirror image that has one extra detail.
definitions.example: A left hand and a right hand are symmetrical, but a left hand with a ring on one finger is asymmetrical.

definitions.definition: A number that represents how much truth a person is willing to accept, ranging from 0 (total rejection) to 1 (full acceptance).
definitions.example: If someone is only half-listening, their acceptance factor might be 0.5.

definitions.definition: The physics theory that describes how quarks and gluons interact via the strong nuclear force.
definitions.example: QCD explains why protons and neutrons stick together inside an atom's nucleus.

definitions.definition: Stored energy that an object has because of its position or condition, waiting to be released.
definitions.example: A ball held above the ground has potential energy because gravity can pull it down.

definitions.definition: Tiny particles that are the building blocks of protons and neutrons.
definitions.example: Quarks are like the LEGO bricks that make up the bigger pieces inside an atom's nucleus.

definitions.definition: The force that pulls quarks back together when they try to separate, like an invisible rubber band.
definitions.example: Imagine two magnets pulling apart, but the farther they go, the stronger the pull back.

definitions.definition: The rule that quarks can never be isolated alone; they are always stuck together in groups.
definitions.example: You can't have a single quark by itself, just like you can't have a single north pole without a south pole.

definitions.definition: A number that tells how strong a force is between two particles or objects.
definitions.example: A strong magnet has a high coupling constant; a weak one has a low coupling constant.

definitions.definition: The pull-back force in a relationship when two people are separated, like the tension in a promise that keeps them connected.
definitions.example: When a close friend moves away, the covenant tension is the feeling that keeps you in touch.

definitions.definition: A number that represents how much a relationship is damaged by betrayal or rejection, reducing the force of love.
definitions.example: If someone breaks a promise, the betrayal factor goes up and the relationship weakens.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; things tend to get messier over time.
definitions.example: Your bedroom naturally gets messier over time unless you clean it.

definitions.definition: A system that does not exchange energy or matter with anything outside it.
definitions.example: A sealed thermos of hot coffee is a closed system because no heat or liquid gets in or out.

definitions.definition: The direction of time that we experience, defined by the fact that entropy always increases.
definitions.example: You can tell a video is playing forward because a dropped glass shatters, not unshatters.

definitions.definition: A measure of spiritual or moral disorder in a person's life that tends to increase over time.
definitions.example: Small bad choices add up, making it harder to do the right thing later.

definitions.definition: Energy added to a system from outside to change its state.
definitions.example: Pushing a stalled car is external work that gets it moving again.

definitions.definition: Unearned help or favor from God that can change a person's spiritual state.
definitions.example: Getting a second chance you didn't deserve is like receiving grace.

definitions.definition: A measure of how much uncertainty or information is in a message or set of possibilities.
definitions.example: A coin flip has high Shannon entropy because you're uncertain; a coin that always lands heads has zero.

definitions.definition: A list or graph that shows how likely each possible outcome is.
definitions.example: A dice roll has a probability distribution where each number 1-6 has a 1/6 chance.

definitions.definition: A Greek word meaning 'Word' or 'Reason'; in Christian theology, it refers to Jesus Christ as the divine principle through which the universe was created.
definitions.example: The Logos is like the blueprint or code that the universe runs on.

definitions.definition: A measure of how complex a piece of data is, based on the length of the shortest computer program that can produce it.
definitions.example: A simple pattern like 'ABABAB' has low Kolmogorov complexity; random letters have high complexity.

definitions.definition: A part of an equation that represents something being added or generated from within the system.
definitions.example: A fountain adds water to a pool; the fountain is the source term.

definitions.definition: A quantity that stays the same for all observers, even if they are moving at different speeds.
definitions.example: The speed of light is a Lorentz invariant because everyone measures it to be the same.

definitions.definition: A combined measure of distance and time between two events that all observers agree on.
definitions.example: Two people might disagree on how far apart events are in space or time, but they agree on the spacetime interval.

definitions.definition: Einstein's theory that the laws of physics are the same for all observers moving at constant speed, and that the speed of light is constant.
definitions.example: Special relativity explains why time slows down for astronauts traveling near the speed of light.

definitions.definition: A property that does not change even when other things change.
definitions.example: The number of sides of a square is invariant even if you rotate or move it.

definitions.definition: A measure of the real, shared experience between two people that captures the depth of their relationship.
definitions.example: Two friends might remember the same event differently, but the time they spent together is their relational proper time.

definitions.definition: A mathematical factor that represents whether both parties freely choose to be in a relationship.
definitions.example: A handshake only works if both people agree to shake; that agreement is the consent term.

definitions.definition: The fundamental equation of quantum mechanics that describes how a quantum system changes over time.
definitions.example: Schrödinger's equation predicts where an electron is likely to be found around an atom.

definitions.definition: A description of all the possible properties a quantum particle can have at a given time.
definitions.example: An electron's quantum state includes its possible positions, speeds, and spins.

definitions.definition: The ability of a quantum particle to be in multiple states at the same time until it is measured.
definitions.example: A spinning coin is in superposition of heads and tails until it lands.

definitions.definition: A formula that calculates the probability of finding a quantum particle in a particular state when measured.
definitions.example: The Born rule tells you the chance of finding an electron at a specific spot.

definitions.definition: A number that represents how strongly a person commits to a belief or outcome, influencing the result.
definitions.example: If you truly believe you will pass a test, your faith commitment factor is high.

definitions.definition: The moment when a quantum system in superposition settles into a single definite state after measurement.
definitions.example: When you open the box with Schrödinger's cat, the cat's state collapses to either alive or dead.

definitions.definition: A type of radioactive decay where a neutron turns into a proton, releasing an electron and an antineutrino.
definitions.example: Beta decay is one way that unstable atoms become more stable.

definitions.definition: One of the four fundamental forces, responsible for certain types of radioactive decay.
definitions.example: The weak force is what makes some atoms radioactive and powers the sun.

definitions.definition: A particle in the nucleus of an atom that has no electric charge.
definitions.example: Neutrons help hold the nucleus together by balancing the repulsion between protons.

definitions.definition: A positively charged particle in the nucleus of an atom.
definitions.example: The number of protons determines what element an atom is.

definitions.definition: A tiny negatively charged particle that orbits the nucleus of an atom.
definitions.example: Electrons are responsible for electricity and chemical bonds.

definitions.definition: The antimatter counterpart of a neutrino, a nearly massless particle released in beta decay.
definitions.example: Antineutrinos are ghostly particles that barely interact with anything.

definitions.definition: A process where a quark changes from one type (flavor) to another, like a down quark becoming an up quark.
definitions.example: Flavor-changing decay is like a LEGO brick changing color while staying the same shape.

definitions.definition: Atoms of the same element that have an unstable nucleus and decay over time.
definitions.example: Carbon-14 is a radioactive isotope used to date ancient artifacts.

definitions.definition: How fast a radioactive substance decays, measured by the number of decays per second.
definitions.example: A high decay rate means the substance is very radioactive and doesn't last long.

definitions.definition: A complex mathematical method used in quantum field theory to predict particle interactions.
definitions.example: Physicists use quantum field-theoretic calculations to predict what happens when particles collide.

definitions.definition: A mathematical term that represents a person's free choice to sin or not.
definitions.example: The will factor is like a switch that lets you choose between right and wrong.

definitions.definition: A measure of how well all parts of a system fit together in a unified, orderly way.
definitions.example: A well-organized team has high coherence because everyone works together smoothly.

definitions.definition: A mathematical space that includes all possible positions and states of a system.
definitions.example: For a moving particle, configuration space includes every possible location it could be.

definitions.definition: A mathematical operation that adds up infinitely many tiny pieces to find a total.
definitions.example: An integral can find the total distance traveled by adding up tiny steps over time.

definitions.definition: A mathematical term added to a spiritual equation that represents human choice, making it different from the physical version.
definitions.example: The free-will modifier is like an 'if-then' statement that lets a person choose the outcome.

definitions.definition: A system where each part is defined in terms of itself or other parts, creating a loop.
definitions.example: A mirror reflecting another mirror creates a self-recursive image that goes on forever.

definitions.definition: The main equation of the framework that combines all ten laws into one formula for total coherence.
definitions.example: The master equation is like the final score that sums up all the individual game stats.

definitions.definition: An equation that describes how a quantity changes over time or space.
definitions.example: A differential equation can describe how the temperature of a cup of coffee cools down.

definitions.definition: A system that changes over time according to fixed rules.
definitions.example: The weather is a dynamic system because it changes based on temperature, pressure, and wind.

definitions.definition: A system where each variable's change depends on the others, creating a feedback loop.
definitions.example: In an ecosystem, the number of rabbits affects the number of foxes, which affects the rabbits again.

definitions.definition: A state where a system is balanced and not changing over time.
definitions.example: A seesaw with equal weights on both sides is in equilibrium.

definitions.definition: In Christianity, the rescue of a person's soul from sin and its consequences, leading to eternal life with God.
definitions.example: Salvation is like being saved from a sinking ship and brought to safety.

definitions.definition: An equation that combines all forces or domains into one description.
definitions.example: A unified field equation would be like a single rule that explains gravity, magnetism, and love all at once.

definitions.definition: A mathematical function that measures how well something is being used or received.
definitions.example: A car's fuel efficiency function tells how many miles per gallon it gets.

definitions.definition: The mathematical condition that must be met for salvation to be possible, requiring an infinite source of grace.
definitions.example: The soteriological limit is like needing an endless fuel supply to keep a spaceship running forever.

definitions.definition: The study of salvation, especially in Christian theology.
definitions.example: Soteriology asks questions like 'How are people saved?' and 'What does salvation mean?'

definitions.definition: A mathematical proof that the ultimate foundation of any system cannot be proven from within that system.
definitions.example: You can't use a ruler to prove the ruler is exactly one foot long; you need something else.

definitions.definition: A basic statement that is accepted as true without proof, used as a starting point for reasoning.
definitions.example: In geometry, 'a straight line is the shortest distance between two points' is an axiom.

definitions.definition: The most basic thing that everything else depends on, which cannot itself depend on anything else.
definitions.example: The foundation of a house is the ground that supports the whole building.

definitions.definition: A statement that follows directly from a previously proven statement.
definitions.example: If all squares are rectangles, a corollary is that all square corners are right angles.

definitions.definition: A famous theorem by Kurt Gödel showing that any consistent mathematical system cannot prove its own consistency.
definitions.example: Gödel's theorem means that math can't prove that math itself is free of contradictions.

definitions.definition: Something we are so sure of that we act on it every day, even if we can't prove it formally.
definitions.example: You are operationally certain that the sun will rise tomorrow, even though you can't prove it.

definitions.definition: A situation where the universe seems to be arranged in a way that is the opposite of what you'd expect.
definitions.example: It's cosmic irony that the tools we use to seek proof of God cannot reach Him.

definitions.definition: A statement that has been proven to be true using logic and axioms.
definitions.example: The Pythagorean theorem is a proven rule about right triangles.

definitions.definition: Something created by a process or system, not the original thing itself.
definitions.example: A fossil is an artifact of a once-living creature, not the creature itself.

definitions.definition: A series of logical requirements that any ultimate foundation must satisfy.
definitions.example: A constraint chain is like a checklist: the ground must be non-physical, necessary, etc.

definitions.definition: Not made of matter or energy; existing outside the physical universe.
definitions.example: Thoughts and numbers are non-physical; you can't weigh or touch them.

definitions.definition: Something that does not depend on anything else for its existence; it just exists necessarily.
definitions.example: A rock is contingent because it could be broken; a non-contingent thing cannot not exist.

definitions.definition: Something that could
